hooks.text: A monster solar storm missed erasing our modern world by nine days.
A record-breaking superstorm hit us, yet nobody on Earth noticed.
What missed wiping out our power grids by only nine days?

title: The Solar Storm That Missed Earth
description: In July 2012, a solar superstorm traveling 2,000 kilometers per second missed Earth by just nine days, narrowly avoiding a global catastrophe.

beats.text: A monster solar storm missed erasing our modern world by nine days.
beats.visual: NASA SDO satellite capture of a giant solar flare, 2012

beats.text: In July 2012, the Sun launched a massive eruption matching the strongest storm ever recorded.
beats.visual: SOHO spacecraft view of an intense coronal mass ejection, 2012

beats.text: This blast traveled over two thousand kilometers per second, four times faster than a typical storm.
beats.visual: Artist illustration of a coronal mass ejection traveling through space, NASA
queries: coronal mass ejection space illustration NASA

beats.text: It achieved this record speed because another eruption four days earlier had cleared its cosmic path.
beats.visual: Solar Dynamics Observatory view of Sunspot Active Region 11520, 2012

beats.text: A direct hit would have crippled global power grids and water pumps, costing over two trillion dollars.
beats.visual: Illustration of Earth's magnetosphere being compressed by a solar storm, NASA

beats.text: Instead, NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft took the hit and survived to show us what we missed.
beats.visual: Artist concept of NASA's STEREO spacecraft in orbit around the Sun, NASA

beats.text: Physicist Pete Riley calculated a twelve percent chance a similar storm strikes Earth every decade.
beats.visual: Graphic of Carrington-class solar storm probability per decade, NASA

beats.text: We survived only because the erupting region of the Sun was no longer pointed directly at us.
beats.visual: Visualization of the 2012 solar storm path missing Earth, NASA
